name: Kokota
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Palmer, Bill. 2002. 'Kokota'. In John Lynch, Malcolm Ross & Terry Crowley (eds), The Oceanic Languages, pp. 498-524. Richmond: Curzon. (author's own sketch; primary description by the grammar's author)
catalog_quote: Stress in Kokota is characterised by considerable variation, to the extent that a single speaker may assign stress variably to words with certain syllable structures. This results from changes that are under way in the stress assignment regime. The regular stress assignment regime involves feet parsed from left to right, so stress is counted from the left margin of the root. Stress is trochaic, meaning that the first and every second subsequent syllable/mora is stressed. (The final syllable/mora in words with an odd number of syllables/moras is not stressed, however, because the final odd syllable/mora is not assigned to any foot.) Primary stress is assigned to the rightmost stressed syllable/mora. This regime is most clearly illustrated in roots with only light syllables - i.e. syllables with only one mora each: ... /ka.me/ 'hand' /ma.ka.si/ 'bonito' /di.hu.na.re/ 'be rough' /pa.ra.ha.…

audit.reasoning: Quote confirmed verbatim at the stated pages in the held djvu-text excerpt of Palmer 2002, and the held Palmer 1999 thesis ch.3 (24 pp. dedicated to stress and prosody) independently states the same regime: left-to-right trochees from the root's left edge, rightmost foot = primary, final odd unit unfooted, older speakers moraic trochees (CVV heavy) vs younger speakers syllabic trochees, prefixes/proclitics/reduplication outside the domain, suffixes/enclitics inside. The 'weight-hedged' classification directly encodes the author's own statement of a change in progress between a quantity-sensitive and a quantity-insensitive foot type, so it is the faithful coding. All descriptive literature on Kokota is by Palmer; the only unheld item is his 2009 published grammar (paywalled), a revision of the held thesis.
